mcqs.question: Two pointers i and j scan sorted arrays A and B. What determines which pointer advances on a given step?
options: i and j always advance together on every step
Whichever array has more remaining elements advances
Random choice, since both eventually reach the end
Whichever pointer's current value is smaller (behind) advances, since it can't match anything further back
mcqs.explanation: The rule is comparative, not positional: the pointer sitting on the smaller value is the one that's behind and needs to catch up, so it advances while the other holds. Advancing both unconditionally, picking by remaining count, or choosing randomly would all break the O(n+m) correctness argument.

mcqs.question: In the in-place "Merge Sorted Array" problem, why must the merge walk pointers from the back of the arrays rather than the front?
options: Because sorted arrays are always easier to traverse in descending order
Because nums1's trailing space must be filled first before any comparisons can happen
Merging from the front would overwrite nums1 elements that haven't been read yet, since the output shares the same array
Because Python arrays are only efficiently iterable in reverse
mcqs.explanation: Writing from the front into nums1 would clobber values still needed for later comparisons, since the merged output occupies the same memory as one of the inputs. Working from the back writes only into space that's already been read or was originally unused padding, which has nothing to do with array direction preferences or Python specifics.

mcqs.question: In the Is Subsequence two-pointer solution, why does pointer j advance on every iteration while pointer i only advances on a match?
options: j tracks progress through t, which is scanned unconditionally, while i only represents progress once a needed character of s has actually been found
It's an arbitrary implementation choice with no effect on correctness
i advances slower because s is guaranteed to be sorted
Advancing j every time avoids an off-by-one error at the end of the loop
mcqs.explanation: j must scan every character of t regardless of outcome, since a match could appear anywhere; i should only move when s actually makes progress, which happens exactly on a match. The choice is load-bearing for correctness, not arbitrary, and neither string needs to be sorted for this pattern.

mcqs.question: The two-pointer intersection algorithm is run on two unsorted arrays containing the same set of values. What happens?
options: It can return an incomplete or wrong result, because 'a[i] < b[j], advance i' stops being a valid inference without sorted order
It throws a runtime exception immediately
It still works correctly but takes O(n²) time instead of O(n)
It works correctly as long as both arrays are the same length
mcqs.explanation: The whole 'advance whichever side is behind' logic depends on sorted order making 'behind' a meaningful, monotonic concept; without it, the comparison no longer proves anything about the rest of the array, so real intersections can be missed. There's no exception thrown, no complexity change, and equal length doesn't rescue the algorithm.

mcqs.question: The two-pointer intersection code (advance both pointers by one on a match, record the value once) naturally computes which variant of the problem?
options: The unique-values variant, since duplicates are automatically removed
Neither variant correctly without extra bookkeeping
Only the version where both arrays have distinct elements
The multiplicity variant, where a value appears min(count in A, count in B) times in the output
mcqs.explanation: Because each match consumes exactly one occurrence from each array before advancing, repeated shared values are emitted up to the smaller of their two counts — that's precisely the multiplicity definition, not the dedupe-to-unique one. No extra bookkeeping is needed for that variant, and it isn't limited to arrays with distinct elements.
